q:
The energy diagram describes a reaction A → C that goes through intermediate B. Which statements are true?
I. The reaction has exactly one intermediate.
II. The first step is the rate-determining step.
III. By the Hammond postulate, the first transition state resembles B more than it resembles A.
h: Find the highest point on the curve, then ask whether step 1 is uphill or downhill.
w: I is true: there is one energy minimum (B) between reactants and products, so one intermediate. II is false: the rate-determining step is the one whose transition state is highest on the diagram, and TS2 (18) lies above TS1 (12), so the second step limits the rate. III is true: step 1 is endergonic (A at 0 → B at 5), so by the Hammond postulate its transition state is late and resembles the higher-energy species, B. I and III only.
x: This misses III: an endergonic step has a late transition state that looks like its product, intermediate B.
This misses I: the single minimum between reactants and products is one intermediate.
II is false: TS2 is the highest point on the curve, so step 2, not step 1, is rate-determining.

q: Which carbocations I–III would rearrange to a more stable carbocation by a 1,2-shift?
h: A shift only pays off if the new cation is more substituted (or resonance-stabilized) than the old one.
w: I does not rearrange: the 1-methylcyclopentyl cation is already tertiary, and any hydride shift would make a secondary cation. II does not rearrange to anything better: a hydride shift in the cyclohexyl cation just makes another secondary cyclohexyl cation, identical to the first. III rearranges: the 3,3-dimethylbutan-2-yl cation is secondary, and a 1,2-methyl shift from the adjacent quaternary carbon gives the tertiary 2,3-dimethylbutan-2-yl cation. III only.
x: I is already tertiary; no 1,2-shift can make it more stable.
A hydride shift in the cyclohexyl cation gives another secondary cation of the same structure, so there is no driving force.
Neither I (already tertiary) nor II (shift gives an identical secondary cation) gains stability by shifting.

q:
3-Methylbut-1-ene reacts with HBr (no peroxides). Which statements about the mechanism are true?
I. Protonation of the alkene gives a secondary carbocation first.
II. A 1,2-hydride shift converts that cation into a tertiary carbocation.
III. The major product is 2-bromo-2-methylbutane.
h: Add H<sup>+</sup> by Markovnikov's rule, then look at the carbon next to the cation.
w: I is true: H+ adds to the terminal CH2 (Markovnikov), leaving a secondary cation on C2. II is true: C3 next door is a C–H carbon bearing two methyls, so a 1,2-hydride shift moves the positive charge to C3, a tertiary center. III is true: bromide captures the more stable tertiary cation, giving 2-bromo-2-methylbutane as the major product (2-bromo-3-methylbutane is the minor, unrearranged product). I, II, and III.
x: III is also true: the rearranged tertiary cation is trapped by Br<sup>−</sup>, so the major product carries Br on the tertiary carbon.
II is also true: the hydride shifts from the adjacent tertiary C–H, which is why the product is rearranged.
I is also true: Markovnikov protonation at CH<sub>2</sub> makes the secondary cation before any shift occurs.

q:
1-Bromobutane reacts with NaCN in methanol by SN2. Which changes would increase the rate?
I. Using 1-chlorobutane in place of 1-bromobutane
II. Using DMSO as the solvent in place of methanol
III. Using 1-bromo-2,2-dimethylpropane in place of 1-bromobutane
h: Think about three S<sub>N</sub>2 factors: leaving group, solvent, and crowding at the backside of the carbon.
w: I is false: Cl− is a poorer leaving group than Br− (Br− is the weaker, more polarizable base and its C–Br bond is weaker), so 1-chlorobutane reacts more slowly. II is true: DMSO is polar aprotic; it does not hydrogen-bond to cyanide, so the nucleophile is less solvated and much more reactive. III is false: 1-bromo-2,2-dimethylpropane (neopentyl bromide) is primary but its β-tert-butyl group blocks backside attack, so it reacts far more slowly. II only.
x: I is false: chloride is a worse leaving group than bromide, which slows S<sub>N</sub>2.
III is false: the neopentyl substrate is primary but badly hindered at the backside, so its S<sub>N</sub>2 rate is tiny.
III is false (neopentyl is very hindered) and II is true: a polar aprotic solvent speeds S<sub>N</sub>2 with anionic nucleophiles.

q:
Which reactions give a racemic organic product? (Each substitution follows the mechanism its conditions favor.)
I. Compound I in H2O/acetone, heat
II. Compound II with NaCN in DMSO
III. Compound III with NaCN in DMSO
h: Ask two things for each: does the reaction happen AT the stereocenter, and is the intermediate planar?
w: I is racemic: (S)-3-bromo-3-methylhexane is tertiary, so in aqueous acetone it ionizes (SN1) to a planar tertiary carbocation that water attacks from either face, giving racemic 3-methylhexan-3-ol (in practice with at most a slight excess of inversion). II is not racemic: (R)-2-bromobutane is secondary and cyanide in DMSO is a good nucleophile in a polar aprotic solvent, so SN2 inverts the center and gives optically active (S)-2-methylbutanenitrile. III is not racemic: in (S)-1-bromo-2-methylbutane the substitution happens at the CH2Br carbon, not at the stereocenter, so the product (S)-3-methylpentanenitrile keeps its configuration. I only.
x: II is not racemic: S<sub>N</sub>2 with cyanide in DMSO gives clean inversion, one enantiomer of the nitrile.
III is not racemic: the stereocenter is not the carbon that reacts, so its configuration is untouched.
III keeps its stereocenter (the reaction is at CH<sub>2</sub>Br), and I does racemize through a planar tertiary carbocation.

q:
Which reagent sequences convert (R)-butan-2-ol into (S)-2-bromobutane?
I. PBr3
II. 1. TsCl, pyridine 2. NaBr, DMSO
III. 1. SOCl2, pyridine 2. NaBr, DMSO
h: Count the inversions. Which steps break a bond to the stereocenter, and which only change the O–H?
w: OH and Br are both the top CIP priority, so each inversion of geometry turns R into S. I works: PBr3 converts the OH into a leaving group that bromide displaces by SN2, one inversion → (S). II works: TsCl reacts at oxygen, so the tosylate keeps the R configuration; then Br− displaces tosylate by SN2, one inversion → (S). III fails: SOCl2 with pyridine gives (S)-2-chlorobutane with inversion, and the SN2 by Br− inverts again, so two inversions give (R)-2-bromobutane. I and II only.
x: II also works: tosylation does not touch the C–O bond, so the one inversion comes in the bromide step.
I also works: PBr<sub>3</sub> converts the alcohol to the bromide with a single S<sub>N</sub>2 inversion.
III fails: it has two inversions (SOCl2/pyridine, then Br−), so it returns the R bromide.

q:
Which of these are better leaving groups than chloride ion in an SN2 reaction?
I. HO−
II. TsO− (tosylate)
III. I−
h: Good leaving groups are weak bases. Compare the pK<sub>a</sub> of each conjugate acid with that of HCl.
w: A leaving group is better the weaker it is as a base. I is false: HO− is a strong base (H2O, pKa 15.7), which is why alcohols must be activated before substitution. II is true: tosylate is the conjugate base of a strong sulfonic acid (pKa about −3) and its charge is spread over three oxygens. III is true: HI (pKa about −10) is stronger than HCl, and the large, polarizable I− leaves from a weak C–I bond. II and III only.
x: III is also true: iodide is a weaker base than chloride and the C–I bond is the weakest carbon–halogen bond.
II is also true: tosylate is resonance-stabilized and is one of the best common leaving groups.
I is false: hydroxide is a strong base and a very poor leaving group.

q:
Which substrate/base combinations give 1-methylcyclohexene as the major product?
I. Compound I with NaOCH2CH3
II. Compound II with NaOCH2CH3
III. Compound III with KOC(CH3)3
h: E2 on a cyclohexane needs an axial leaving group and an axial β hydrogen on the neighboring carbon. Then think about base size.
w: I (trans-1-bromo-2-methylcyclohexane) fails: Br is axial only in the chair where the methyl is also axial, so the H on C2 is equatorial and cannot be anti-periplanar; E2 must use C6 and gives 3-methylcyclohexene. II (cis-1-bromo-2-methylcyclohexane) works: with Br axial the methyl is equatorial, so C2 has an axial H anti to Br and E2 forms the more substituted 1-methylcyclohexene (Zaitsev). III fails: with bulky tert-butoxide, the tertiary bromide loses a methyl H, giving mainly the less substituted methylenecyclohexane (Hofmann). II only.
x: I fails: in the trans isomer the C2 hydrogen cannot be anti-periplanar to an axial Br, so 3-methylcyclohexene forms.
III fails: the bulky base removes the most accessible H (on CH<sub>3</sub>), so methylenecyclohexane is the major product.
This reverses the two isomers: the cis compound, not the trans, has an axial C2–H anti to an axial Br.

q:
(2S,3S)-2-Bromo-3-phenylbutane is treated with NaOCH2CH3 in ethanol. Which statements are true?
I. The major alkene is (E)-2-phenylbut-2-ene.
II. The (2S,3R) diastereomer gives the same alkene stereoisomer.
III. In the transition state, the H removed and the Br are syn-periplanar.
h: Draw the conformation with H on C3 anti to Br on C2. Which groups end up on the same side of the new π bond?
w: C3 has only one H, so the Zaitsev product (conjugated, trisubstituted 2-phenylbut-2-ene) forms stereospecifically. III is false: E2 requires the C–H and C–Br bonds to be anti-periplanar. I is true: with H(C3) anti to Br in the (2S,3S) isomer, the C1 methyl on C2 and the phenyl on C3 end up on opposite sides of the new double bond; those are the higher-priority groups on each carbon, so the alkene is (E). II is false: the (2S,3R) diastereomer places the methyl and phenyl on the same side in its anti-periplanar conformation, so it gives the (Z) alkene. Diastereomers give different alkenes in a stereospecific E2. I only.
x: II is false: E2 is stereospecific, so the diastereomer with the opposite configuration at C3 gives the (Z) alkene.
III is false: E2 needs the H and the leaving group anti-periplanar (180°), not syn.
I is true (anti elimination puts CH3 and Ph trans, the E alkene), and II is false.

q:
2-Bromopropane reacts with NaOCH3 in methanol to give a mixture of propene and 2-methoxypropane. Which changes increase the fraction of elimination?
I. Running the reaction at a lower temperature
II. Using KOC(CH3)3 in place of NaOCH3
III. Using 2-bromo-2-methylpropane in place of 2-bromopropane
h: Elimination makes more molecules (higher ΔS), is favored by bulky bases, and wins when the carbon is too crowded for backside attack.
w: I is false: elimination has the larger, more favorable ΔS (more product molecules), so it is favored by higher temperature; cooling increases substitution. II is true: tert-butoxide is a strong but bulky base that cannot easily reach the backside of carbon, so it removes a β H instead. III is true: a tertiary bromide cannot undergo SN2, so a strong base gives almost entirely E2. II and III only.
x: III is also true: tertiary substrates block S<sub>N</sub>2, so a strong base gives E2 almost exclusively.
II is also true: a bulky alkoxide is a poor nucleophile but a strong base, which shifts the ratio toward elimination.
I is false: lowering the temperature favors substitution, because elimination is the entropy-driven pathway.

q: Which alcohols give 2-methylbut-2-ene as the major product when heated with concentrated H2SO4?
h: Follow each cation: does it shift to the tertiary 2-methylbutan-2-yl cation before it loses H<sup>+</sup>?
w: All three funnel to the same tertiary cation, (CH3)2C+CH2CH3, which loses H+ to give the Zaitsev (most substituted) alkene, 2-methylbut-2-ene. I (2-methylbutan-2-ol) forms this tertiary cation directly. II (3-methylbutan-2-ol) forms a secondary cation that undergoes a 1,2-hydride shift to the tertiary cation. III (2,2-dimethylpropan-1-ol) cannot form a primary cation; loss of water is assisted by a 1,2-methyl shift that gives the same tertiary cation. I, II, and III.
x: III also works: the neopentyl alcohol undergoes a methyl shift as water leaves, giving the tertiary cation and then 2-methylbut-2-ene.
II also works: the secondary cation from 3-methylbutan-2-ol undergoes a hydride shift to the same tertiary cation.
II and III also work: both rearrange (hydride shift and methyl shift) to the tertiary 2-methylbutan-2-yl cation.

q:
Which reactions give a meso compound as the product?
I. (Z)-but-2-ene + Br2 in CH2Cl2
II. (E)-but-2-ene + Br2 in CH2Cl2
III. (Z)-but-2-ene + OsO4, then NaHSO3, H2O
h: Decide whether each reagent adds syn or anti, place the two new groups on the cis or trans alkene, and check the product for an internal mirror plane.
w: Br2 adds anti (bromonium ion, backside opening); OsO4 adds syn. I is false: anti addition to the cis alkene gives the chiral (2R,3R)/(2S,3S)-2,3-dibromobutane pair as a racemate. II is true: anti addition to the trans alkene gives (2R,3S)-2,3-dibromobutane, which has an internal mirror plane (meso). III is true: syn addition to the cis alkene puts both OH groups on the same side, giving meso-butane-2,3-diol (2R,3S). II and III only.
x: III is also meso: syn dihydroxylation of a cis alkene gives the (2R,3S) diol with a mirror plane.
II is also meso: anti addition across a trans alkene gives (2R,3S)-2,3-dibromobutane.
I is not meso: anti addition across a cis alkene gives the chiral (R,R) and (S,S) dibromides as a racemate.

q:
Which reagent sequences convert 1-methylcyclohexene into racemic trans-2-methylcyclohexan-1-ol (shown)?
I. H2O, H2SO4
II. 1. mCPBA 2. LiAlH4 3. H3O+
III. 1. BH3·THF 2. H2O2, NaOH
h: The OH ends up on the less substituted alkene carbon, and H and OH end up on the same face. Which sequence does both?
w: The target has OH on the less substituted carbon (anti-Markovnikov) and is trans. I fails: acid-catalyzed hydration goes through the tertiary carbocation and gives 1-methylcyclohexan-1-ol (Markovnikov). II fails: hydride from LiAlH4 opens the epoxide by SN2 at the less hindered secondary carbon, so the oxygen stays on the tertiary carbon and the product is again 1-methylcyclohexan-1-ol. III works: B and H add syn with B on the less substituted carbon; oxidation replaces B by OH with retention, so H (on C2) and OH (on C1) are cis, which puts the CH3 and OH trans. III only.
x: II fails: hydride attacks the less hindered epoxide carbon, leaving OH on the tertiary carbon (1-methylcyclohexanol).
I fails: acid hydration is Markovnikov through a tertiary cation, giving 1-methylcyclohexanol.
II fails, and III works: hydroboration–oxidation is the only anti-Markovnikov, syn route here.

q:
Which reactions give a racemic mixture of chiral products?
I. But-1-ene + HBr
II. Cyclopentene + OsO4, then NaHSO3, H2O
III. Cyclohexene + Br2 in CH2Cl2
h: For each product ask: is it chiral at all? A product with an internal mirror plane is meso, not racemic.
w: I is racemic: Markovnikov addition gives 2-bromobutane, and Br− attacks the planar secondary carbocation from either face, so (R) and (S) form equally. II is not racemic: syn dihydroxylation gives cis-cyclopentane-1,2-diol, a meso compound (achiral, with a mirror plane). III is racemic: anti addition gives trans-1,2-dibromocyclohexane, which is chiral and forms as the (1R,2R)/(1S,2S) pair. I and III only.
x: III is also racemic: trans-1,2-dibromocyclohexane is chiral and both enantiomers form equally.
I is also racemic: 2-bromobutane forms from a planar carbocation attacked on both faces.
II is false: cis-cyclopentane-1,2-diol is meso, so there is no pair of enantiomers.

q: Which alkenes give only one organic product when treated with 1. O3 2. (CH3)2S?
h: Ozonolysis cuts the C=C and makes a C=O on each end. When are both ends part of the same molecule?
w: I gives one product: the double bond is in the ring, so cleavage opens the ring and both carbonyls stay in one chain, 5-oxohexanal (CH3CO(CH2)3CHO). II gives two: 2-methylbut-2-ene splits into acetone and acetaldehyde. III gives two: the exocyclic C=C splits into cyclohexanone and formaldehyde. I only.
x: II gives two products: acetone from the disubstituted end and acetaldehyde from the other end.
III gives two products: cyclohexanone plus formaldehyde from the exocyclic CH<sub>2</sub>.
Only the ring (endocyclic) alkene keeps both new carbonyls in one molecule; III is exocyclic and splits into two compounds.

q:
Which reagent sequences convert propyne into propanal?
I. 1. (Sia)2BH (disiamylborane) 2. H2O2, NaOH
II. H2O, H2SO4, HgSO4
III. 1. H2, Lindlar catalyst 2. BH3·THF 3. H2O2, NaOH 4. PCC
h: An aldehyde needs the oxygen on the terminal carbon: you need an anti-Markovnikov step somewhere.
w: I works: a bulky borane adds once to the terminal alkyne with B on C1; oxidation gives an enol that tautomerizes to propanal. II fails: Hg2+-catalyzed hydration is Markovnikov, putting O on C2 and giving acetone. III works: Lindlar gives propene, hydroboration–oxidation gives propan-1-ol (anti-Markovnikov), and PCC oxidizes the primary alcohol to propanal without going on to the acid. I and III only.
x: III also works: propene → propan-1-ol → propanal, and PCC stops at the aldehyde.
I also works: hydroboration of a terminal alkyne with a bulky borane gives the aldehyde after tautomerization.
II fails: mercury-catalyzed hydration follows Markovnikov's rule and gives the methyl ketone, acetone.

q:
Hex-3-yne is converted to an alkene, and the alkene is then treated as shown. Which sequences give a racemic product?
I. 1. Na, NH3(l) 2. Br2, CH2Cl2
II. 1. H2, Lindlar catalyst 2. Br2, CH2Cl2
III. 1. Na, NH3(l) 2. OsO4, then NaHSO3, H2O
h: First decide which alkene each reduction gives (cis or trans), then whether the second step is syn or anti.
w: Na/NH3 gives (E)-hex-3-ene; Lindlar gives (Z)-hex-3-ene. Br2 adds anti; OsO4 adds syn. I is false: trans + anti gives (3R,4S)-3,4-dibromohexane, a meso compound. II is true: cis + anti gives the chiral (3R,4R)/(3S,4S) dibromide as a racemate. III is true: trans + syn gives (3R,4R)/(3S,4S)-hexane-3,4-diol as a racemate. II and III only.
x: III is also racemic: syn dihydroxylation of the trans alkene gives the chiral (R,R)/(S,S) diol pair.
II is also racemic: anti addition of Br<sub>2</sub> to the cis alkene gives the chiral dibromide pair.
I is false: anti addition of Br<sub>2</sub> to the trans alkene gives the meso dibromide.

q:
Hex-2-yne is to be made from propyne in two steps (deprotonation, then alkylation). Which statements about this plan are true?
I. NaOH is a strong enough base to deprotonate propyne almost completely.
II. NaNH2 deprotonates propyne essentially completely.
III. 2-Bromopropane is as good an alkylating agent here as 1-bromopropane.
h: Compare pK<sub>a</sub> values (terminal alkyne ≈ 25, water ≈ 15.7, ammonia ≈ 38), then think about S<sub>N</sub>2 versus E2 for the acetylide.
w: I is false: water (pKa 15.7) is a much stronger acid than propyne (pKa about 25), so hydroxide cannot deprotonate propyne to any useful extent. II is true: ammonia (pKa about 38) is a far weaker acid than propyne, so amide removes the alkyne C–H essentially completely. III is false: the propynide ion is a strong base, and with a secondary halide it mostly causes E2 (giving propene); the plan needs the primary halide 1-bromopropane, and it gives hex-2-yne only from a straight-chain propyl group anyway. II only.
x: I is false: the equilibrium lies far on the side of propyne and hydroxide, because water is the stronger acid.
III is false: acetylide ions are strong bases and give mainly elimination with secondary halides; 2-bromopropane would also put a branched group on the alkyne.
I is false (water is a stronger acid than propyne, so hydroxide fails), and II is true: amide is a much stronger base than the acetylide.

q:
2-Methylbutane is treated with Br2 and light. Which statements are true?
I. The major product is 2-bromo-2-methylbutane.
II. Each molecule of product requires the absorption of a new photon.
III. Bromination is more selective than chlorination because H abstraction by Br• is endothermic, so its transition state is late and radical-like.
h: Think about how a chain reaction keeps going, and apply the Hammond postulate to the H-abstraction step.
w: I is true: Br• abstracts the tertiary H selectively (tertiary radical most stable), giving 2-bromo-2-methylbutane as the major product. II is false: light only starts the chain by splitting Br2; the two propagation steps (R–H + Br• → R• + HBr; R• + Br2 → R–Br + Br•) regenerate Br•, so one photon can lead to many product molecules. III is true: H abstraction by Br• is endothermic, so by the Hammond postulate the transition state resembles the alkyl radical, and differences in radical stability (3° > 2° > 1°) show up strongly in the rates; the exothermic Cl• abstraction has an early, reactant-like transition state and is much less selective. I and III only.
x: This misses III: the late, product-like transition state is exactly why bromination is so selective.
This misses I: bromination strongly prefers the tertiary C–H, so the tertiary bromide is the major product.
II is false: propagation regenerates Br•, so one photon starts a chain that makes many product molecules.

q: Which alkenes give a single constitutional isomer of allylic bromide with NBS and light (ignore stereoisomers)?
h: Draw the allylic radical and its resonance form. Bromine can bond at either end of the allylic system.
w: I gives two: removing an allylic H from but-1-ene gives a radical delocalized over C1 and C3, so both 3-bromobut-1-ene and 1-bromobut-2-ene form. II gives several: 1-methylcyclohexene has three different allylic positions (the CH3, ring C3 and ring C6), and their radicals are not equivalent. III gives one: the cyclohexenyl radical is symmetric, so bromine at either end of the allylic system gives the same 3-bromocyclohexene. III only.
x: I gives two products: the allylic radical from but-1-ene has unequal ends, giving 3-bromobut-1-ene and 1-bromobut-2-ene.
II gives several products: 1-methylcyclohexene has three nonequivalent allylic positions.
I is wrong (two products from the unsymmetric allylic radical), and III gives one product because its allylic radical is symmetric.

q:
Which reagents convert cyclohexene into cis-cyclohexane-1,2-diol?
I. OsO4 (catalytic), NMO
II. KMnO4, NaOH, H2O, cold
III. 1. mCPBA 2. H3O+
h: Sort the methods into syn and anti dihydroxylations.
w: I works: OsO4 adds both oxygens to one face through a cyclic osmate ester (syn); NMO reoxidizes the osmium so only a catalytic amount is needed. II works: cold, basic KMnO4 also forms a cyclic manganate ester and gives syn addition. III fails: mCPBA gives the epoxide, and acid-catalyzed opening by water occurs from the back face, so the product is trans-cyclohexane-1,2-diol. I and II only.
x: II also works: cold, dilute, basic permanganate is a syn dihydroxylation through a cyclic manganate ester.
I also works: catalytic OsO<sub>4</sub> with NMO as the reoxidant is the standard syn dihydroxylation.
III fails: epoxidation then acid opening is an anti addition and gives the trans diol.

q:
Which sequences convert acetylene into (E)-hex-3-ene?
I. 1. NaNH2 2. CH3CH2Br 3. NaNH2 4. CH3CH2Br 5. H2, Lindlar catalyst
II. 1. NaNH2 2. CH3CH2Br 3. NaNH2 4. CH3CH2Br 5. Na, NH3(l)
III. 1. NaNH2 2. CH3CH2Br 3. NaNH2 4. CH3CH2Br 5. H2, Pt
h: All three build the same alkyne first. The last step decides the outcome.
w: Steps 1–4 are the same in every route: two deprotonation–alkylation cycles add an ethyl group to each end, giving hex-3-yne. I fails: H2 with Lindlar catalyst adds both H atoms syn, giving (Z)-hex-3-ene. II works: dissolving-metal reduction (Na in NH3) goes through a vinyl radical and vinyl anion that adopt the trans arrangement, giving (E)-hex-3-ene. III fails: H2 over Pt reduces the alkyne all the way to hexane. II only.
x: I fails: Lindlar reduction is syn and gives the Z alkene.
III fails: an unpoisoned Pt catalyst reduces the alkyne completely to the alkane.
This reverses the two partial reductions: Lindlar gives the Z alkene, and Na/NH3 gives the E alkene.

q:
Which reagent sequences convert 1-methylcyclohexene into 1-bromo-2-methylcyclohexane (ignore which stereoisomer forms)?
I. HBr, ROOR, hν
II. 1. BH3·THF 2. H2O2, NaOH 3. PBr3
III. HBr (no peroxides)
h: The Br must end up on the less substituted alkene carbon. Which routes are anti-Markovnikov?
w: I works: under peroxides Br• adds to the less substituted carbon so that the more stable tertiary radical forms; that radical takes H from HBr, putting Br on C2 of the original alkene (anti-Markovnikov). II works: hydroboration–oxidation gives trans-2-methylcyclohexan-1-ol, and PBr3 converts the secondary alcohol to the bromide with inversion (so this route gives specifically the cis bromide, but the constitution is right). III fails: ionic HBr addition goes through the tertiary carbocation and gives 1-bromo-1-methylcyclohexane (Markovnikov). I and II only.
x: II also works: anti-Markovnikov alcohol, then PBr<sub>3</sub>, puts Br on the secondary carbon next to the methyl.
I also works: radical addition of HBr is anti-Markovnikov because the tertiary radical forms on the way.
III fails: without peroxides HBr adds through the tertiary carbocation and gives 1-bromo-1-methylcyclohexane.

q:
Which reagents convert pentan-1-ol into pentanal without significant further oxidation?
I. Na2Cr2O7, H2SO4, H2O
II. KMnO4, NaOH, heat; then H3O+
III. PCC, CH2Cl2
h: Over-oxidation of an aldehyde goes through its hydrate, which needs water.
w: I fails: chromic acid in water oxidizes the primary alcohol to the aldehyde, which forms a hydrate and is oxidized on to pentanoic acid. II fails: hot permanganate is a strong oxidant that also takes a primary alcohol to the carboxylic acid. III works: PCC in anhydrous CH2Cl2 stops at the aldehyde, because no water is present to form the hydrate that would be oxidized further. III only.
x: I fails: aqueous chromic acid over-oxidizes a primary alcohol to the carboxylic acid.
II fails: hot KMnO<sub>4</sub> oxidizes the primary alcohol all the way to pentanoic acid.
I fails (aqueous chromic acid gives the acid), and III works: PCC in dry CH<sub>2</sub>Cl<sub>2</sub> stops at the aldehyde.

q:
Which methods give tert-butyl ethyl ether, (CH3)3COCH2CH3, as the main product?
I. (CH3)3CO− K+ + CH3CH2Br
II. CH3CH2O− Na+ + (CH3)3CBr
III. 2-Methylpropene + CH3CH2O− Na+ in ethanol
h: In a Williamson synthesis the alkoxide attacks by S<sub>N</sub>2. Which carbon can be attacked from the back? And can an alkoxide add to an ordinary C=C?
w: I works: this is a Williamson ether synthesis with the alkyl group on the primary halide, so SN2 at the unhindered CH2 gives the ether. II fails: SN2 at a tertiary carbon is impossible, and ethoxide acts as a base, so E2 gives 2-methylpropene. III fails: an unactivated alkene is electron-rich and does not react with a nucleophile such as ethoxide (adding ethanol across the C=C needs an electrophile, for example H+ or Hg2+). I only.
x: II fails: a tertiary bromide with a strong base gives E2 (2-methylpropene), not substitution.
III fails: an alkoxide cannot add to an ordinary alkene; the C=C is a nucleophile, not an electrophile.
This reverses the Williamson rule: the tertiary piece must be the alkoxide and the halide must be primary, so I works and II fails.
